extracted.intended_audience: attorneys/practitioners before the USPTO, OED counsel, and counsel handling reciprocal disciplinary matters
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedures the USPTO Director uses to decide whether to impose reciprocal discipline based on a state's disciplinary adjudication, and the substantive ethical rules and sanctioning standards that support such discipline. Includes the burden on a practitioner to avoid identical discipline and related publication/notification requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocal discipline standard (37 C.F.R. § 11.24(d))
rubrics_metrics.description: The USPTO Director shall consider any timely filed response and shall impose the identical public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification unless the practitioner clearly and convincingly demonstrates, and the USPTO Director finds there is a genuine issue of material fact that one of the listed grounds exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text mirrors Selling v. Radford; practitioner bears the burden to show a genuine issue of material fact by clear and convincing evidence. The Office is not a court of review to re-litigate the underlying tribunal's findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground to avoid reciprocal discipline: deprivation of due process
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine issue of material fact that 'the procedure elsewhere was so lacking in notice or opportunity to be heard as to constitute deprivation of due process' will preclude imposition of identical reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must prove lack of adequate notice or hearing opportunity by clear and convincing evidence. Mere disagreement with outcome is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground to avoid reciprocal discipline: infirmity of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine issue of material fact that 'there was such infirmity of proof establishing the conduct as to give rise to the clear conviction that the Office could not, consistently with its duty, accept as final the conclusion on that subject' will preclude reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This requires demonstrating clear weakness or insufficiency in the proof of the misconduct; federal review is narrow and does not permit collateral attack on factual findings without clear and convincing evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground to avoid reciprocal discipline: grave injustice
rubrics_metrics.description: A genuine issue of material fact that 'the imposition of the same public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension or disciplinary disqualification by the Office would result in a grave injustice' will preclude identical discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analysis focuses on whether the severity of the punishment 'fits' the misconduct; courts look to whether the state sanction was within the appropriate range, and consider mitigating and aggravating factors. Extraordinary circumstances is not a recognized test under § 11.24.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ground to avoid reciprocal discipline: challenge to characterization of sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Any argument that the practitioner was not publicly censured, publicly reprimanded, placed on probation, disbarred, suspended or disciplinarily disqualified may raise a genuine issue of material fact under § 11.24(d)(1)(iv).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Must be established by clear and convincing evidence; simply disputing labels without showing a bona fide factual dispute will generally fail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden and standard of proof for respondent
rubrics_metrics.description: In reciprocal discipline cases, it is the respondent attorney's burden to demonstrate, by clear and convincing evidence, that one of the Selling elements (due process, infirmity of proof, grave injustice) precludes reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal courts and the USPTO apply a narrow standard; the Office will not act as a court of review to discover error in the original proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: ABA Standards for Imposing Lawyer Sanctions — Standard 6.12 (presumptive suspension)
rubrics_metrics.description: Standard 6.12 states suspension is generally appropriate when a lawyer knows that false statements or documents are being submitted to the court or that material information is actually being withheld, and takes no remedial action, and causes injury or potential injury to a party or causes an adverse or potentially adverse effect on the legal proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although 6.12 presumes suspension, parties and tribunals may agree to or impose lesser sanctions based on mitigating factors (e.g., absence of prior discipline, cooperative attitude). The Office considers the ABA Standards as relevant in assessing appropriate discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigating factors that may reduce sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors such as absence of a prior disciplinary history, free and full disclosure to the disciplinary board, cooperative attitude toward proceedings, and other mitigation may support a lesser sanction than the presumptive penalty.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigation was used here to reduce presumptive suspension to reprimand plus one-year probation and CLE; the presence of mitigation does not by itself preclude reciprocal discipline if the underlying sanction is within the appropriate range.

rubrics_metrics.name: Aggravating factors supporting greater sanction
rubrics_metrics.description: Knowingly withholding material information from a tribunal, causing harm to legal proceedings (e.g., necessitating a new trial), and conduct violating the duty to the legal system are aggravating circumstances that support more severe sanctions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Office and state tribunals will weigh harm to the proceeding and the knowing character of the conduct when deciding appropriate discipline.

rubrics_metrics.name: Impact of consent agreements and voluntary admissions
rubrics_metrics.description: A practitioner's voluntary entry into a consent agreement admitting misconduct and agreeing to sanctions (with waiver of adjudicatory hearing and other defenses) undermines claims of grave injustice and generally precludes escape from reciprocal discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts routinely find no grave injustice where the underlying discipline was voluntarily agreed to; signing a consent agreement and failing to timely object is a significant factor against relief.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific rules violated cited as basis for discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The Arizona Consent Agreement and Decision cited violations of Rule 42, Ariz. R. Sup. Ct. Ethical Rules 3.2 (expediting litigation), 3.3 (candor toward the tribunal), and 8.4(d) (engaging in conduct that is prejudicial to the administration of justice); USPTO discipline was predicated upon a violation of 37 C.F.R. § 11.804(h) (being reprimanded on ethical grounds by a duly constituted authority of a State).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Substantive ethical violations (e.g., candor to the tribunal, withholding material information) form the factual/legal basis for state discipline that triggers reciprocal proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural mechanics of USPTO reciprocal discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office of Enrollment and Discipline (OED) Director may file a Request for Reciprocal Discipline; the USPTO issues a Notice and Order; the respondent may file an Answer/Response; the OED Director may respond; the USPTO Director considers the filings and issues a Final Order imposing identical discipline unless one of the § 11.24 defenses is proven.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respondent must raise timely objections and may petition for judicial review (see below). The Director may also order conditions such as probation and CLE, and require proof of compliance to OED.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of discipline and publication/notification requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: The Director may impose public censure, public reprimand, probation, disbarment, suspension, or disciplinary disqualification and shall publish a Notice in the Official Gazette materially consistent with the order; the OED Director must give notice pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.59 to state disciplinary agencies, courts of admission, and the public.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Notice should set out the basis for discipline and the relevant decision; disciplinary decisions are available through the OED FOIA Reading Room. Respondent must also comply with duties enumerated in 37 C.F.R. § 11.58 during any probation/suspension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to judicial review and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.57(a) and 35 U.S.C. § 32, review of the final decision by the USPTO Director may be had by a Petition filed with the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia within thirty (30) days after the date of the order recording the Director's action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local rules (e.g., E.D. Va. Local Civil Rule 83.5) apply; practitioners should note the strict 30-day filing deadline for judicial review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope of practitioners subject to USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct
rubrics_metrics.description: Practitioners admitted to practice law in a state and authorized to practice before the Office in trademark and non-patent matters pursuant to 37 C.F.R. § 11.14(a) are subject to the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct at 37 C.F.R. § 11.101 et seq.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State admission and authorization to practice before the Office bring attorneys under USPTO disciplinary jurisdiction for matters involving professional conduct.
